Reading

The innocent reading first. A quoted string that exists in two places returns the poem at both, with its author, its date and its record number, three days after it was published. The composer counts: ten lines, a seven-beat second and third line, four e-i pairs and then six, three lols closing line 8, then lil alone and lol alone. Each count is right against the seated text. It reads the poem as moving from babble to 'recognizable English text-speak (lol) and slang (lil)', and then sets it in the sound-poetry line as the piece that 'reverses that trajectory', letting the word come out of the sound.

  • EVERY COUNT IS RIGHT. Ten lines; seven beats in lines 2 and 3; four pairs then six; three lols at the end of line 8; lil, then lol.
  • TWO SOURCES, BOTH THE AUTHOR'S. The Hello Poetry post and the record's AXN page; no third party.
  • THE SEARCH PAGE DOES NOT KNOW THE STRING. 'Did you mean "la la ka ka la, error, karir"' stands above an Overview that answers the string as typed.
  • ONE OVERLAP, ONE SLIP OF NAMING. Line 8 falls in two movements; 'New Human 2' is bracketed as the deposit.
  • THE ARCHIVE ENTERS THE READING. 'anchoring the poem in the Alexanarch archive with cryptographic metadata and ending on lol' is given as the poem's digital turn.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

An address claimed while it is still empty of anything else: the string resolves to the poem alone, attributed, on the first run, and the search page itself does not yet know the words ('Did you mean ... error, karir'). Three things to mark. The record page the composer cites is the AXN resolver, dated in the card 26 November; the record's own date is 25 November, which the composition gives. 'New Human 2' is given in brackets after the deposit number as if it named the deposit; it is the series. The third movement is given as lines 5 to 8 and the fourth as lines 8 to 10, so line 8 is counted twice. The closing offers name 'his Glyphic Checksum series' and 'cryptographic hashes' paired with the poems: the archive's apparatus has entered the reading of a ten-line sound poem. The comparison table's entries for Ball, Schwitters, Tzara and Isou are the composer's general knowledge and were not checked here.

[QUERENT] analyze structure and patterns [COMPOSER] "la la ka ka la, wrrir, akerir" is built on a four-stage phonetic progression across ten lines. The poem transitions from percussive, staccato syllables to long vowel runs, and finally into resonant, word-like vocalizations. Macro-Structure (The Four Movements) • Movement 1: Percussive Opening (Lines 1–3). The poem establishes a crisp rhythmic pulse using the open vowel la and the velar stop ka. Line 1 introduces two rolled, trill-like interruptions (wrrir, akerir), while lines 2 and 3 settle into a steady, seven-beat chant (la la la la ka la ka), shifting from period-separated staccato (la.la.la.la) to smooth spacing. • Movement 2: Vowel Expansion (Line 4). The steady beat breaks open into two sustained, oscillating vowel runs built from alternating e and i sounds. The first run (loeieieiei) uses four pairs, and the second (leieieieieiei) stretches to six pairs, mimicking a sustained vocal trill or ululation. • Movement 3: Nasal & Back-Vowel Shift (Lines 5–8). The pitch drops from bright front vowels (e, i) to rounded back vowels (o) paired with alveolar nasals (n) and liquids (l). Phrases like lo laye-lo lan, lo-oanno, and no no low create a heavier, humming cadence that resolves into repeating oh lo loops. • Movement 4: Semantic Emergence (Lines 8–10). Closing the l and o sounds with a final l transforms pure glossolalia into recognizable English text-speak (lol) and slang (lil). After repeating lol three times at the end of line 8, the poem isolates lil on line 9 and lol on line 10 as single-word conclusions. Key Phonetic & Visual Patterns • Consonant Anchoring: The liquid consonant L acts as the structural backbone across all ten lines, evolving from an initial onset (la, lo) into a bracketing frame (lil, lol). • Typographic Pacing: Punctuation and spacing act as musical notation. Commas create brief pauses in line 1, periods enforce clipped pauses in line 2, and hyphens in lines 5–6 (laye-lo, lo-on, lo-oanno) bind syllables into single breath units. • Pre-Linguistic to Digital Arc: The overall trajectory mimics vocal development, moving from infant-like babbling (la, ka) and raw vocal play (wrrir, eieiei) into modern internet vernacular (lil, lol). While classic sound poems sought to strip away standard language to reach a primal or purely musical state, Lee Sharks' piece reverses that trajectory by letting modern internet shorthand (lil, lol) emerge out of pre-linguistic babble. "Lettrist Hypergraphics" Isidore Isou (1940s–1950s) Lettrism Micro-phonetic notation using clicks, coughs, sighs, and invented symbols. Key Connections & Departures • Musical Notation via Typography: Like Kurt Schwitters' Ursonate—which uses spacing, capitalization, and punctuation to dictate tempo and breath—Sharks uses periods (la.la.la.la), hyphens (lo-oanno), and vowel repetition (leieieieieiei) as a performance score. • Glossolalia and "Zaum": The Russian Futurists (such as Velimir Khlebnikov and Aleksei Kruchenykh) coined zaum ("beyond sense") to describe a universal, trans-rational language of pure sound. Sharks' opening la and ka patterns tap into this same primal, infant-babble universality before narrowing into English slang. • The Digital Turn: Classic Dada and Lettrist poets used sound poetry to rebel against print culture and industrial modernity. By anchoring the poem in the Alexanarch archive with cryptographic metadata and ending on lol, Sharks bridges raw bodily vocalization with algorithmic and digital communication.
